findings.description: Sandbox escape / arbitrary code execution in PIL.ImageMath.eval(): user-controlled expression is passed to builtins.eval(), and the name-based "scan" sandbox can be bypassed because caller-supplied environment keys whitelist arbitrary attribute names; the globals dict also misspells __builtins (missing trailing __), causing CPython to inject the full builtins module (CVE-2023-50447, fixed in 10.2.0).
findings.reasoning:
`eval(expression, _dict={}, **kw)` at src/PIL/ImageMath.py:225-263 compiles and executes the caller-supplied `expression` string with `builtins.eval()` (line 259). The only protection is the `scan()` loop, which rejects identifiers found in `code.co_names` unless the same string is a key of `args`, where `args = ops | _dict | kw`. This is a name blacklist implemented as a whitelist of caller-controllable keys, so:
1) Any environment dict / keyword argument key supplied by the caller (e.g. `__class__`, `__base__`, `__subclasses__`, `__globals__`) automatically whitelists that attribute access for the expression.
2) Therefore an attacker who controls the expression and can pass kwargs (or an env dict) can walk the object graph: `().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()[...].__init__.__globals__['exec'](...)`, needing only substring keys in the environment — which are supplied by the very same call. String subscript keys are constants (`co_consts`), not `co_names`, so `['exec']`/`['system']` are never scanned.
3) Independently, the globals mapping passed to eval is `{"__builtins": {"abs": abs}}` — note the typo `__builtins` instead of `__builtins__`. Because the `__builtins__` key is missing, CPython automatically inserts the *real* builtins module, so the intended restriction to `abs` only does not apply at all; any name that passes `scan()` resolves to the full builtin set.
The repository version is 10.1.0 (src/PIL/_version.py), i.e. the last release before the 10.2.0 fix for CVE-2023-50447. The test suite only validates the trivial direct cases (`exec('pass')`, lambdas — Tests/test_imagemath.py:56-63), which do not cover the environment-key bypass. Realistic impact: any application that forwards user-supplied math expressions (common for image-processing services / templating over PIL) is exposed to full remote code execution with the privileges of the service.

evidence.code_context: src/PIL/ImageMath.py:225-263 — def eval(expression, _dict={}, **kw): args = ops.copy(); args.update(_dict); args.update(kw); ... compiled_code = compile(expression, "<string>", "eval"); scan checks `if name not in args and name != "abs": raise ValueError`; then out = builtins.eval(expression, {"__builtins": {"abs": abs}}, args)
evidence.dataflow_analysis: CodeQL codeFlows show: Tests/test_imagemath.py:61/63 (test_prevent_exec expression parameter) -> ImageMath.eval expression param (src/PIL/ImageMath.py:225) -> builtins.eval sink (src/PIL/ImageMath.py:259). The same flow exists for any external caller passing a user-controlled string to ImageMath.eval(expression).
evidence.notes: src/PIL/_version.py:2 => __version__ = "10.1.0" (vulnerable range, CVE-2023-50447 fixed in 10.2.0). In-tree tests only cover direct `exec('pass')` and nested lambda variants; the `args` key whitelisting bypass and the `__builtins` typo are not mitigated. Ops whitelist contains names like abs/int/float/convert/min/max which are also resolvable through the auto-injected real builtins module.

findings.description: os.system() in ImageShow.Viewer.show_file executes a command string built from the temp file path (marked # nosec); not attacker-controlled
findings.reasoning: show_file() is only reached from show_image(), and the `path` passed in is the return value of save_image() -> image._dump(), i.e. a temporary file name generated internally by Pillow (mkstemp-style, no user/server-controlled input). The subclasses' get_command() implementations quote the path (MacViewer uses quote(file); WindowsViewer wraps in double quotes) and are local-developer convenience viewers (show(). Not exploitable from an image payload; the call is annotated with # nosec because the sink is inherent to the design. Classifying as false positive for CWE-78 (residual hardening: prefer subprocess list form).

evidence.dataflow_analysis: grep for 'os.system' returned only src/PIL/ImageShow.py:116. Path originates from Viewer.save_image -> image._dump() which creates an internal temp file name; no external input reaches `path`.
evidence.notes: Developer-facing image viewer helper; not reachable from untrusted image data. Marked fp; recommend subprocess list form as hardening.

findings.description: pickle.load() in test helper reading a file written moments earlier by the same test (round-trip test data)
findings.code_snippet:
def helper_pickle_file(tmp_path, pickle, protocol, test_file, mode):
    # Arrange
    with Image.open(test_file) as im:
        filename = str(tmp_path / "temp.pkl")
        if mode:
            im = im.convert(mode)

        # Act
        with open(filename, "wb") as f:
            pickle.dump(im, f, protocol)
        with open(filename, "rb") as f:
            loaded_im = pickle.load(f)
findings.reasoning: This is inside a pytest helper in the test suite. The pickle file is created by the same test via pickle.dump into a pytest tmp_path immediately before being loaded. No untrusted input reaches this sink; the vulnerability is not exploitable in production. Consistent with guidance to classify non-exploitable test code as false positives.

evidence.code_context: helper_pickle_file(tmp_path, pickle, protocol, test_file, mode) writes temp.pkl then reads it back to assert image equality
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source is the test's own pickle.dump output; no external dataflow into pickle.load
evidence.notes: Test-only round-trip serialization test; production library code unaffected

evidence.code_context:
def test_pickle_la_mode_with_palette(tmp_path):
    filename = str(tmp_path / "temp.pkl")
    with Image.open("Tests/images/hopper.jpg") as im:
        im = im.convert("PA")
    for protocol in range(0, pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL + 1):
        im._mode = "LA"
        with open(filename, "wb") as f:
            pickle.dump(im, f, protocol)
        with open(filename, "rb") as f:
            loaded_im = pickle.load(f)
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source of pickled bytes is the test's own pickle.dump call on a PIL Image object -> temp file in tmp_path -> read back. No external input.
evidence.notes: Test-only code, not shipped in the PIL package; safe round-trip serialization test.

findings.description: Dynamic __import__ in Image.init() iterates a hardcoded, module-level plugin list (_plugins), not attacker-controlled input
findings.reasoning: The import name is f"PIL.{plugin}" where `plugin` comes from `_plugins` imported from `.` (PIL/__init__.py). grep confirms `_plugins` is defined only in src/PIL/__init__.py line 25 as a literal list of ~40 hardcoded plugin names (BlpImagePlugin, BmpImagePlugin, ...). No user/image-controlled data reaches this loop, so an attacker cannot influence the imported module name. Module-name namespace is also fixed to the "PIL." prefix, so even arbitrary suffix would be confined to the PIL package. Not exploitable.

evidence.code_context:
src/PIL/__init__.py:25:
_plugins = [
    "BlpImagePlugin",
    "BmpImagePlugin",
    ... (hardcoded literal list)
]
src/PIL/Image.py:56 imports _plugins from '.'; Image.py:358-362 loops over it calling __import__(f"PIL.{plugin}", ...).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: No source reaches the import name: the iterable is a constant list defined at module load time. There is no path from file/image data, query params, or any other untrusted input into _plugins.
evidence.notes: grep_search for '_plugins' returns only 3 hits: Image.py:56 (import), Image.py:358 (loop), PIL/__init__.py:25 (literal definition). No mutation of _plugins observed.

findings.description: check_module() __import__ uses a module name from a hardcoded dict, validated before use
findings.reasoning: The `module` variable is a value from the statically-defined `modules` dict (PIL._imaging, PIL._tkinter_finder, PIL._imagingft, PIL._imagingcms, PIL._webp). The attacker-controlled `feature` argument is only used as a dict key and is rejected with ValueError if not in `modules`; it never becomes the module name. All importable names are literals inside the PIL package.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: feature (untrusted) -> membership check in constant dict -> dict lookup returns constant string -> __import__. The untrusted value never flows into the import name, only into the dict key comparison.
evidence.notes: Even if the dict lookup succeeded with arbitrary data, the result would be a fixed literal; unknown features raise ValueError early.
